chunks: It's a peripheral that takes a byte from the CPU, shifts it out one bit at a time on a TX pin, and does the reverse on an RX pin, turning the incoming bits back into a byte.
The important word is asynchronous. There's no clock wire between the two chips. Instead both sides agree ahead of time on a baud rate, say 115200, and each uses its own clock.

To keep them lined up, every byte is wrapped in a frame: the line idles high, a start bit pulls it low to say here comes a byte, then the data bits go out least-significant first, and a stop bit takes it high again.
The receiver uses that falling start edge to line up its sampling.
In the simplest form it's two data wires, TX and RX, plus a shared ground, and the two chips cross them so one side's TX goes to the other side's RX.

It's slow compared with SPI, but it's cheap, dead simple, and everywhere: debug consoles, GPS modules, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi modules, and the USB-to-serial cable you plug in on day one of any board bring-up."
